description: For NASA Space Apps 2026, I'm developing astronaut health monitoring software focused on physiological trends, personalized baselines, and AI-assisted decision support. My expertise includes Python, machine learning, neuroscience, and data analysis. I'm open to collaborators with skills in software development, aerospace medicine, human factors, AI, UX/UI design, and space exploration.
summary:
CAELIVIS is an offline-first, non-diagnostic crew health research prototype designed to explore how astronauts could document, visualize, and better understand personal health observations during long-duration space missions.

The platform combines six capabilities: Mission Health Overview, Daily Health Check-In, Personal Baseline & Trends, Health Insights & Alerts, NASA Research Data Explorer, and Privacy & Communications.

A key feature is its integration of historical NASA Open Science Data Repository research from the SpaceX Inspiration4 mission (OSD-569). The explorer presents 28 complete blood count sample records from four coded participants across seven documented collection timepoints. These historical measurements are clearly distinguished from synthetic demonstration records and crew-entered check-ins.

CAELIVIS explores personalized health observation, descriptive trend visualization, spaceflight hazard awareness, offline-first data handling, and simulated communication delays. Its goal is to contribute to research into accessible, crew-centered health monitoring for future exploration missions.
details:
CAELIVIS, developed by NeuroViu Frontier, is an offline-first astronaut health intelligence research prototype designed around the physiological, psychological, and operational challenges of long-duration human spaceflight.

Space exploration introduces unique demands on human health. Astronauts must manage changes in cardiovascular indicators, sleep, physical activity, mood, fatigue, and general well-being while operating in environments where immediate communication with Earth may be limited.

CAELIVIS brings health observations, personal trend visualization, educational spaceflight health insights, and research data exploration together in one mission-focused application.

How It Works

The application contains six interconnected sections:

  1. Mission Health Overview: An interactive astronaut visualization that allows users to explore available health observations and their recorded provenance.
  2. Daily Health Check-In: A structured interface for entering demonstration health observations, including heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, sleep, mood, and other indicators.
  3. Personal Baseline & Trends: Interactive visualizations and descriptive comparisons that help users explore changes relative to their own recorded observations.
  4. Health Insights & Alerts: Educational information connecting health observations with relevant human-spaceflight hazards and appropriate follow-up considerations.
  5. NASA Research Data Explorer: An interactive explorer for historical complete blood count measurements from the SpaceX Inspiration4 research study, NASA OSDR accession OSD-569.
  6. Privacy & Communications: An offline-first demonstration of local record storage, simulated message queuing, and communication-delay considerations. No actual outbound transmission is implemented.

NASA Research Data Integration

CAELIVIS incorporates the public NASA Open Science Data Repository dataset, Whole Blood Measurements from the SpaceX Inspiration4 Mission.

The integrated transformed dataset contains:

  • 28 sample records
  • Four coded participants
  • Seven documented collection timepoints
  • Complete blood count measurements

The application presents these historical research measurements with their source attribution and limitations. They are not live spacecraft telemetry or continuous in-flight monitoring.

Benefits and Intended Impact

CAELIVIS explores how crew-centered health observation tools could support:

  • More organized documentation of health observations.
  • Awareness of individual patterns and changes over time.
  • Improved accessibility to health information during extended missions.
  • Research into personalized astronaut health monitoring.
  • Understanding of communication and data-handling constraints in deep-space environments.
  • Future integration with wearable physiological monitoring technologies.

The intended impact is to provide a foundation for exploring accessible, individualized health-monitoring concepts for future human spaceflight.

Technology and Development

CAELIVIS was developed as a Python-based Streamlit application.

Technologies and development components include:

  • Python application logic.
  • Streamlit interactive interface.
  • Pandas-based research data processing.
  • Plotly interactive data visualization.
  • Local JSON storage and offline-first workflows.
  • Inline SVG astronaut visualization.
  • NASA Open Science Data Repository research data.
  • GitHub for source-code hosting and version control.
  • Github Copilot

The prototype uses clearly identified synthetic demonstration records, crew-entered demonstration observations, and historical NASA research measurements.

It does not connect to astronaut wearable sensors, collect live spacecraft telemetry, or provide validated medical decision support.

Creativity and Innovation

CAELIVIS combines personal health observation, descriptive trend exploration, historical spaceflight research data, and offline-first design in one interactive platform.

Its approach emphasizes individual variability rather than assuming that all astronauts share identical health baselines.

The interactive astronaut visualization provides an accessible way to explore recorded observations, while the NASA Research Data Explorer connects the prototype to actual historical human-spaceflight research.

Design Considerations

Development considered:

  • Human factors: Readable interfaces and accessible health information.
  • Scientific accuracy: Clear data provenance and research limitations.
  • Individual variability: Personal observation histories rather than generalized medical thresholds.
  • Operational constraints: Limited connectivity and simulated communication delays.
  • Privacy: Local data storage with transparent security limitations.
  • Safety: Non-diagnostic presentation and appropriate human medical oversight.
  • Scalability: Potential future integration with wearable sensors and additional research datasets.

CAELIVIS is a research and educational prototype. It does not diagnose, predict, prescribe treatment, or replace qualified medical personnel.
